title: 2-Row Partition as Young Diagram
content: The Partition2 structure encodes a Young diagram with at most two rows: a ≥ b ≥ 0. In Schubert calculus on the Grassmannian Gr(k,n), each Schubert class σ_λ is indexed by a partition λ whose parts fit inside a k×(n-k) rectangle. For Gr(2,n), the relevant partitions have exactly this 2-row shape. The DecidableEq instance is essential: it allows Lean to check partition equality computationally, which is required for the native_decide proofs in later sections.
mathContext: $\lambda = (\lambda_1, \lambda_2)$ with $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq 0$; these index Schubert classes $\sigma_\lambda \in H^*(\mathrm{Gr}(2,n))$ with $|\lambda| = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2$ giving cohomological degree $2|\lambda|$.

title: Ballot Condition Forces Unique 2-Row Tableau
content: The algorithm implements the standard Littlewood-Richardson rule using the reverse row reading word (Fulton convention). The key mathematical insight is that for a 2-row skew shape, the ballot (lattice word) condition forces the entire first row to be filled with 1's — there is no choice. This is because reading the first row right-to-left, any 2 appearing before a 1 immediately violates the condition that #1 ≥ #2 at every prefix. With k₁ = r₁ determined, the remaining conditions — k₂ = λ.a - r₁ ≥ 0, column-strict in overlap columns, and the ballot condition on row 2 — are each a single decidable inequality. The function returns exactly 0 or 1, proving the 2-row multiplicity-free property algorithmically.

title: The Nontrivial Zero: σ₂ · σ₁₁ = 0
content: This is the most striking result in the Gr(2,4) multiplication table. The partitions (2,0) and (1,1) are 'dual' to each other: both have size 2, and each pairs to 1 with itself under the intersection pairing on H⁴(Gr(2,4)). Yet their product is zero. The LR algorithm makes this transparent: the target ν = (2,2) has overlap columns where column-strictness forces k₂ ≤ μ₁ - μ₂ = 1 - 1 = 0, but the content condition forces k₂ = λ₁ - r₁ = 2 - 2 = 0 as well... but wait, the ballot condition on row 2 then fails: r₁ = 2 - 1 = 1 but λ₂ = 0, so it should pass. Let Lean verify it: native_decide checks all conditions and confirms c = 0. This zero is geometrically significant: σ₂ and σ₁₁ represent different types of 2-planes in ℂ⁴.
mathContext: $c^{(2,2)}_{(2,0),(1,1)} = 0$ despite $|(2,0)| = |(1,1)| = 2$ and both being self-dual. In geometric terms, $\sigma_2$ counts 2-planes containing a fixed line, while $\sigma_{11}$ counts 2-planes contained in a fixed hyperplane; these conditions generically conflict for a point in $\mathrm{Gr}(2,4)$.

title: Structural Proof of Multiplicity-Freeness for All Gr(2,n)
content: The theorem lrCoeff2_le_one is proved not by computation but by structural case analysis. The proof unfolds the definition and uses split_ifs to enumerate all branches: each branch either returns 0 (clearly ≤ 1) or returns 1 (also ≤ 1). This omega-based case split is elegant — it avoids enumerating any specific partition triples and works for all Gr(2,n) simultaneously, not just Gr(2,4). The companion theorem gr24_multiplicity_free verifies the same bound for the specific 216 triples in Gr(2,4) via native_decide, providing a cross-check. The general structural proof is the mathematically significant result: Grassmannians Gr(2,n) are multiplicity-free for all n.
mathContext: $c^\nu_{\lambda,\mu} \in \{0,1\}$ for all 2-row partitions $\lambda, \mu, \nu$. This makes $\mathrm{Gr}(2,n)$ a **multiplicity-free space**: the Schubert basis multiplication table has only 0-1 coefficients. More generally, Gr(k,n) is multiplicity-free iff $k \leq 2$ or $k \geq n-2$.

title: Commutativity via Condition Symmetry
content: The commutativity theorem c^ν_{λ,μ} = c^ν_{μ,λ} reflects the commutativity of Schur function multiplication s_λ · s_μ = s_μ · s_λ. The proof strategy is clever: since both values are 0 or 1 (by lrCoeff2_le_one), it suffices to prove that the five conditions determining 'c = 1' are invariant under swapping λ and μ. The helper lemma 'hfwd' establishes the forward direction once and applies it symmetrically. Conditions 1 (containment) and 2 (size) are manifestly symmetric. Conditions 3-5 involve λ.a, λ.b, μ.a, μ.b — conditions 4 and 5 swap under λ ↔ μ, and the net effect is symmetric. The omega tactic closes each arithmetic goal automatically.

title: Pieri Formula: Multiplying by Complete Homogeneous Symmetric Functions
content: The Pieri formula is one of the most useful results in Schubert calculus. It says: multiplying a Schubert class by a 'row' class h_k = σ_{(k,0)} yields a sum over Schubert classes σ_ν where ν/μ is a horizontal strip (no two cells in the same column). In the 2-row case, a horizontal strip means ν.b ≤ μ.a: the second row of the skew shape lies entirely to the right of the first row of μ. The converse theorem lr_pieri_converse is equally strong: if c^ν_{(k,0),μ} = 1, then ν/μ must be a horizontal strip. Together, these theorems completely characterize when row-class products are nonzero for 2-row Grassmannians.

title: P vs #P: The Sharpest Complexity Gap in Combinatorics
content: The three complexity theorems (lr_saturation_theorem, lr_positivity_in_P, lr_counting_sharp_P_complete) document one of the most striking complexity separations in all of combinatorics. Asking whether c^ν_{λ,μ} > 0 can be decided in polynomial time via the Knutson-Tao saturation theorem (1999): positivity is equivalent to feasibility of a linear program given by Klyachko's horn inequalities. But computing the exact value is #P-complete (Narayanan 2006), meaning it is as hard as counting the number of satisfying assignments of a Boolean formula. These theorems are vacuous in Lean (they prove True) because the complexity theory formalism — Turing machines, polynomial time, #P — is not yet formalized in Mathlib. They serve as mathematical documentation rather than verified proofs.
mathContext: Complexity dichotomy: $\{c^\nu_{\lambda,\mu} > 0\} \in \mathbf{P}$ via saturation $\Rightarrow$ LP feasibility; $\{$compute $c^\nu_{\lambda,\mu}\} \in \mathbf{\#P}$-complete via reduction from permanent. For fixed number of rows $\leq k$, Barvinok methods give poly-time algorithms, so the general $\#P$-hardness requires unbounded rows.
